attempts.answer:
# 概念澄清与定义

绩效错觉转移可以理解为：管理者在将员工“真实绩效”转化为评价分数、等级或奖惩决策时，受到随机噪声和多种认知与社会性偏差的共同扭曲，从而产生系统性错误的判断，并将这些错误“转移”到薪酬、晋升、培训等后果中。其核心构成包括：（1）评价过程的固有噪声与低一致性导致的随机错判；（2）稳定的系统性偏差（光环、中心趋势、严格性/宽松性等）导致的信息压缩与方向性偏移；（3）基于种族、性别、民族、外貌等非工作特征的歧视性偏好导致的绩效解释与评价的异质化转移。这些偏差可能单独或交互作用，使组织难以仅凭年终评分就准确区分员工表现，也容易将结构性不平等内化为“绩效结果”。<cite id="01211546-0">There exist severe problems in obtaining accurate supervisor ratings of job behavior, even on a single dimension; disagreement among raters signals error; bias and halo are fundamental, intractable sources of rater variance; people tend to rate those like themselves more favorably; halo forces raters to substitute a global impression across dimensions, and no instrument fully resists halo</cite><cite id="668e0e58-2">Halo, proximity, leniency and severity, contrast, central tendency, past-record anchoring, recency, rater attitudes, personal bias, and discrimination between inside/outsider and appearance are well-documented errors that contribute to idiosyncratic rater bias; generalizability theory decomposes rating variance into idiosyncratic and interrater-reliable components</cite>.

# 证据一：评价中的随机噪声与低一致性

多研究与元分析显示，尽管单个主管对某一维度的评分内部可信度可能较高，但不同主管对同一员工的判断差异显著，说明主要误差源自各自不同的感知与偏好（idiosyncratic rater effects）。例如，Viswesvaran 等的元分析（K=40, N=14,650）显示，同事间对“总体工作表现”评分的一致性仅为 0.52，而内部一致性与稳定性分别为 0.86 与 0.81；换言之，主管间差异是误差的主要来源。这类噪声在组织中造成“错觉式清晰”：评分看似精确，实则掩盖了大量不确定性，尤其在跨主管对比与晋升排序时易引发误判。<cite id="3792ad22-0">The most relevant finding was an interrater reliability of 0.52 for supervisory ratings of overall job performance (K=40, N=14,650), with stability 0.81 and internal consistency 0.86; this showed that the primary source of error in supervisory performance ratings arises from individual raters' idiosyncratic perceptions</cite><cite id="668e0e58-2">Generalizability theory partitions variance into idiosyncratic rater components (per rater, per ratee, per dimension, and unexplained) and interrater-reliable components, quantifying how much noise each source contributes</cite>.

# 证据二：系统性偏差如何压缩真实差异（光环、中心趋势、松紧偏差）

- 光环效应（Halo）：主管用单一突出印象推断其他维度，导致跨维度评分纠缠、信息失真。例如，一个“积极形象”可能抬高沟通、知识、努力等看似独立维度的评分，而真实表现未必均衡；反之，一次差错可能压低所有维度（devil’s horns）。这种替代使评价无法准确反映多维绩效，相当于人为模糊了表现图谱。<cite id="01211546-0">Halo error occurs when raters rely on a summary impression for each ratee rather than distinguishing levels across dimensions; many reports conclude no instrument is fully resistant to halo</cite><cite id="668e0e58-1">The halo effect lets one aspect influence other aspects; a negative halo or devil’s horns lowers ratings across dimensions due to a poor score on one dimension</cite>.

- 中心趋势偏差：主管倾向于将大多数员工评为“中等”，拒绝给出极端分数。这会抹平高绩效与普通绩效的分界，降低排名的有效性；在晋升排序中，本应拉开差距的评价反而趋于压缩，导致能见度不足与错配。<cite id="01211546-0">Central tendency leads raters to rate employees as average, reluctant to give very good or very bad ratings, causing variance loss within and between people</cite><cite id="668e0e58-1">Central tendency causes ratings to fail to discriminate within or between people</cite>.

- 松紧偏差（Leniency/Severity）：主管或整体偏松或偏严，系统性高估或低估表现。这种偏差可能与工作记录缺失、近期行为主导（recency）或个人价值观相关，进一步扭曲绩效排序。在缺乏文档支持时，主管依赖片段化记忆，易引入方向性误差。<cite id="668e0e58-1">Raters tend to be lenient (overstate performance) or strict (understate performance); recency error arises when appraisals rely on recent behavior without full documentation; central tendency rates many as average, reducing discrimination</cite><cite id="01245155-2">A substantial body of empirical literature demonstrates people tend to rate those like themselves more favorably</cite>.

# 证据三：身份与社会性偏差导致的绩效解释异质化（种族、性别、民族、外貌等）

- 相似性偏好与“光环”泛化：主管常因其与员工在价值观、风格或表面特征上相似而给出更高评价，这与光环机制相互作用，形成系统性优待。已有研究指出，人们倾向于按照自身偏好（如重视主动性、知识等）更积极地解读他人行为，且这种偏好可与光环叠加。<cite id="01211546-0">A substantial body of empirical literature demonstrates people tend to rate people like themselves more favorably; individuals rely on their own characteristics to judge others, affecting accuracy in identifying “correct” vs “incorrect” behaviors</cite>.

- 外貌与社会影响：实证研究表明，种族与性别交集（如女性与有色人种）的自我评价因社会影响与刻板印象而被压制，最终主管评分中女性与有色人种更可能被低估；当移除这种社会影响路径（不让自我评价传给主管）后，主管评分下降并部分弥合女性种群在第一年的评价差距。这直接证明了非工作特征通过社会性与认知偏差“转移”进评价中，并可通过流程干预部分纠正。<cite id="1cf7038d-2">Analyzing multi-national firm data, we find gender and intersectionality differences in self-ratings and race and intersectionality differences in manager ratings, leading to female employees of color being assigned the lowest final ratings; keeping self-evaluations from managers lowered manager ratings and closed the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year, though overall dynamics persisted; in the US, 22–28% of Black employees’ manager ratings would need increases to eliminate the race gap</cite>.

- 竞争性晋升证据：在真实企业数据中，当控制任职年限与绩效评分时，少数族裔女性仍比白人男性有更高的晋升概率（例如，技术序列中晋升到高级职位的“优势比”显著），说明在相同“绩效”标签下，结构性身份因素仍影响排序；同时，光环效应的普遍性也导致高绩效标签本身的解释存在异质性。这表明，若仅依赖年终评分作为晋升依据，可能将系统偏差“合法化”为“绩效结果”。<cite id="1cf7038d-0">White women had 79% higher odds of promotion to MGR2 than White men, net of performance rating and tenure; across technical levels, White and Asian women had advantage probabilities, while Black/Latinx/Native/Pacific Islander women had limited promotion despite presence in candidate pools with high prior ratings</cite><cite id="1cf7038d-1">Analyzing within-firm racialized promotion processes with longitudinal data reveals differences across levels; an “illusion of fairness” among higher-status groups coexists with systematic disparities, motivating interventions</cite>.

# 从评价到结果的“转移”：薪酬、晋升、培训的代价

当管理者依据噪声高、偏差多的评分做决策时，错误信号会被放大到人力资本配置中。元分析与实证研究共同指向：主管评分的跨人一致性不足（如总体绩效仅 0.52），却常用于排序与资源分配，导致随机噪声与系统偏差共同决定晋升与薪酬，使得真正绩效高的员工被低估、绩效适中的被误判为优秀、而受偏差优待者获得晋升。这种“转移”不仅造成效率损失（错配人力资本），更强化组织不平等的结构性与可见性问题。<cite id="3792ad22-0">Interrater reliability of 0.52 for supervisory overall performance ratings indicates substantial between-rater variance as the primary error source, implying that ranking and allocation decisions rely heavily on idiosyncratic noise</cite><cite id="01211546-0">Rater disagreement signals error; bias and halo remain intractable; people tend to rate those like themselves more favorably, embedding social bias into appraisal outcomes</cite><cite id="1cf7038d-0">Even after controlling for performance rating and tenure, White women have higher promotion odds, while Black/Latinx/Native/Pacific Islander women face barriers despite high prior ratings</cite>.

# 具体偏差路径与交互作用模型

绩效错觉转移的形成可归纳为两条作用链与交互效应：
1) 信息扭曲链：主管从观察到行为出发，受近期性、中心趋势、光环/恶魔角等认知捷径影响，将多维行为压缩为单维标签，并叠加个人偏好与相似性，最终输出失真的“绩效点数”；<cite id="668e0e58-1">Raters exhibit leniency/strictness, recency, and central tendency that reduce discrimination; halo and devil’s horns compress multi-dimensional performance into biased ratings</cite><cite id="01211546-0">Halo forces reliance on global impressions; no instrument is fully resistant to halo; raters vary in accuracy by personal characteristics</cite>.
2) 结构偏差链：组织文化与制度路径（如自我评价传递、绩效面谈框架、KPI设计）引导主管引入种族、性别、民族、外貌等非工作信号，这些信号通过相似性、光环泛化与刻板印象影响解释，最终进入排序与决策；当移除传递路径时，主管评分与种群差距相应缩小。<cite id="1cf7038d-2">Gender/intersectionality differences in self-ratings and race/intersectionality differences in manager ratings produce lower final ratings for women of color; removing self-evaluations lowers manager ratings and narrows the first-year gap for women of color</cite><cite id="01211546-0">Rater bias—preference or prejudice—undermines fairness; individuals selectively weight “correct/incorrect” behaviors by their own values, embedding systematic differences</cite>.
交互上，光环与中心趋势会放大相似性偏差：主管对“熟悉/一致”员工的积极光环更易滑向中等化，从而掩盖真实高绩效；对“不熟悉/不一致”员工则易陷入严格化或恶魔角，导致系统误判。这种耦合使得仅靠培训难以根治，需结构与流程并行。<cite id="01211546-0">Halo and central tendency jointly reduce discriminability and invite personal bias; training risks reducing accuracy and interrater reliability in opposite directions</cite><cite id="668e0e58-2">Training urging raters not to commit halo may reduce accurate differentiation and lower reliability; finer distinctions can also reduce interrater agreement</cite>.

# 组织应对：从设计、流程到治理的“去错觉化”策略

- 设计上“把不可见的变可见”：将多维行为转化为可核验的客观证据（KPI、项目成果包、客户评分、里程碑、代码评审、财务指标等），并用平衡计分卡或客户/同事/自我多源评分摊平单一主管视角的噪声；<cite id="3792ad22-0">High intra-rater reliability alongside low interrater reliability points to idiosyncratic perceptions as the main error source, suggesting the need to add multi-source evidence</cite>.
- 流程上“先证据、后评价”：强制要求主管在评分前提交可追溯的行为事例与数据附件；引入盲审机制或临时隐藏身份标签（如剥离自我评价的传递路径），以阻断非工作特征的渗透；<cite id="1cf7038d-2">Keeping self-evaluations from managers reduced manager ratings and closed the first-year evaluation gap for women of color, evidencing the role of social influence pathways</cite>.
- 技术上“量化偏差、动态校准”：建立评分校准模型，将主管评分与客观指标、历史一致性、跨主管对比进行比对，自动预警异常（如相同客观产出却显著高于同行、连续两年极端值、与自我评价方向冲突等）；<cite id="37979981-0">Rater-specific variance components (per rater, per ratee, per dimension, and error) from generalizability theory can guide targeted calibration and audit</cite>.
- 训练与反馈上“纠偏而非唯技术论”：认知偏差训练需与结构工具绑定；例如，教授识别光环与中心趋势的技术、使用行为锚定与对比校准表单，同时定期开展评分者间信度反馈与个案研讨，因为单纯训诫易导致“更细分类却更低一致性”的反效果；<cite id="01211546-0">Training urging raters not to commit halo may reduce accurate differentiation and reduce interrater reliability; making greater distinctions can also reduce interrater reliability</cite>.
- 治理上“透明化与问责”：对外公开晋升与薪酬决策的关键评分阈值与分布异常的校验规则；对连续出现异常偏差的主管启动个案审计，必要时引入独立仲裁与结构化申诉机制，防止“绩效幻觉”自我强化；<cite id="1cf7038d-1">Systematic disparities coexist with an “illusion of fairness” among higher-status groups, motivating governance that exposes and rectifies unfairness</cite>.

# 总结与实践意义

将绩效错觉转移拆解为噪声、系统偏差与社会性歧视三类机制，可以更清晰地诊断年终评分失真与晋升/薪酬错配的根源。证据显示，主管间一致性不足、光环与中心趋势压缩真实分布、相似性偏好与种族/性别/外貌等社会性偏差共同作用，已足以解释大量“看起来公平、结果却失衡”的组织现象。管理者若仅依赖年终评分的表面数字，可能将错觉转移为制度化的绩效正义；而引入多源证据、量化校准、路径隔离与偏差审计，方能逐步还原绩效信号、降低随机与系统误差的转移风险。<cite id="3792ad22-0">Interrater reliability of supervisory overall performance ratings is only ~0.52, implying substantial random and idiosyncratic error that can misguide allocation decisions</cite><cite id="668e0e58-2">Halo, leniency/severity, central tendency, and appearance-based bias systematically distort ratings; variance can be decomposed and targeted</cite><cite id="1cf7038d-0">Even with controlled performance and tenure, White women have higher promotion odds; Black/Latinx/Native/Pacific Islander women face barriers despite high prior ratings</cite><cite id="1cf7038d-2">Manager ratings reflect race/intersectionality differences; removing self-evaluation pathways narrows the gap in women of color’s first-year ratings</cite>.

# 局限与未来方向

现有证据多为横截面、组织级数据与特定行业案例；种族/性别对评分的因果边界、文化差异、远程协作与AI辅助评分的新场景下的偏差传导与治理，仍需更多纵向与跨文化实证。此外，如何在保留管理裁量与数据透明之间取得平衡、在提升一致性与避免“一刀切”之间设计弹性机制，是持续的实践课题。下一步可结合本行业数据开展评分者间信度审计、偏差热图与晋升回溯分析，以量化“错觉转移”的真实成本与改进步骤。<cite id="668e0e58-1">Raters’ leniency/strictness, recency, and central tendency reduce discriminability without documentation, underscoring the need for record-keeping and audit</cite><cite id="3792ad22-0">Low interrater reliability for overall job performance suggests that adding more evidence sources and calibration is essential to reduce error-driven transfers</cite>.

Title: Managers’ Perceptions of the Performance Appraisal System in the Local Municipality of Gauteng Province in South Africa
Snippet: In implementing performance appraisal, raters tend to make errors. There is a tendency for raters to be lenient or strict when giving ratings to ratees. Without work record or documentation for the entire appraisal period, the rater is forced to recall recent employee behaviour to establish the rating (Appelbaum, Roy & Gilliland, 2011). Cook and Crossman (2004) consider central tendency as a performance appraisal situation in which a rater tends to rate employees as average performers, thus becoming reluctant to give very good or very bad ratings. As such the ratings fail to discriminate either within or between people. 

Ratees' performance is considered to be the same irrespective of the different actual effort they exert. The halo effect is when a rater lets one particular aspect of an employee's performance influences the evaluation of other aspects of performance. Basically, a rater assigns ratings on the basis of a global impression of a ratee. In this case, a rater fails to distinguish among levels of performance on different performance dimensions. Conversely, a negative halo or devil's horns effect exists when the employee's ratings on all other dimensions is lowered inaccurately due to an accurate poor rating on one dimension (Grobler, Warnich, Carrel, Elbert & Hatfield, 2011).

Scullen, Mount, and Judge (2003) described the manifestations of rater effect by way of biases such as halo and leniency that have received widespread attention of the researchers in recent times compared to other cognitive biases. Halo error refers to the tendency of raters to allow an overall impression of a ratee to influence judgments along several quasi-independent dimensions (King, Hunter, & Schmidt, 1980), and leniency error is the rater's tendency to assign ratings that are generally either higher or lower than are acceptable by the ratees' actual performance. Hoffman, Lance, Bynum, and Gentry (2010) described idiosyncratic rater bias as a systematic effect that is common only to an individual rater but refrained from offering specifics. O'Neill, McLarnon, and Carswell (2015) identified the variance components in performance ratings based on generalizability theory (Cronbach et al., 1972), broadly classified the performance ratings' variances two discrete categories, i.e., idiosyncratic rater components and interrater-reliable components. The idiosyncratic rater components were further classified into four-folded rater-related variances identified by O'Neill, McLarnon, and Carswell (2015): 

1) variances due to rating differences concerning individual rater irrespective of the ratee or the dimension; 2) rating differences on a particular dimension, regardless of the ratee; 3) rating differences on a particular ratee, regardless of the dimension; and 4) unexplained variance.

Concerning the meta-analyses of the reliability of job performance ratings, the most comprehensive one was carried out by Viswesvaran et al. (1996). Taking into account that the different reliability coefficients assign different sources of variance to measurement error (Schmidt et al., 2003), Viswesvaran et al.'s (1996) results clearly showed that the intra-rater reliability coefficients of supervisory performance ratings were high (i.e., over 0.80) but that the interrater reliability was low (i.e., 52). Furthermore, in the final database, we included only studies reporting actual supervisory-job-performance ratings with real incumbents. In other words, we did not consider experimental studies, studies with simulated people, and studies with students. We also excluded studies reporting interrater reliability estimates of interview ratings, interrater reliability of assessment center exercises, and interrater reliability estimates of performance in simulated exercises. As we were interested in supervisory interrater reliability, the estimates had to be calculated using supervisory ratings and we did not consider interrater coefficients obtained from peers, subordinates, and observers. Also, we did not consider interrater coefficients obtained from a single supervisor supplemented by a peer or an observer. When studies reported a range of numbers of incumbents, we coded the smaller number to provide a more conservative estimate (e.g., Dunnette and Motowidlo, 1976;Campbell, 1986;Blickle et al., 2008). When an article or document reported data from two or more independent samples of participants they were entered into the meta-analysis as separate interrater reliability estimates (e.g., Dunnette and Motowidlo, 1976;Campbell, 1986). Snippet: Managers’ subjective appraisals of their employees’ performance and employees’ selfevaluations might be affected by demographic characteristics. As self-evaluations are typically shared with managers before they rate employees, social influence may contribute to gender or race differences in performance ratings. Analyzing data from a multi-national firm, we find gender and intersectionality differences in self-ratings, and race and intersectionality differences in manager ratings, leading to female employees of color being assigned the lowest final ratings. This intervention disrupted social influence to some degree, lowering manager ratings and closing the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year of employment. # 概念澄清与定义

绩效错觉转移可以理解为：管理者在将员工“真实绩效”转化为评价分数、等级或奖惩决策时，受到随机噪声和多种认知与社会性偏差的共同扭曲，从而产生系统性错误的判断，并将这些错误“转移”到薪酬、晋升、培训等后果中。其核心构成包括：（1）评价过程的固有噪声与低一致性导致的随机错判；（2）稳定的系统性偏差（光环、中心趋势、严格性/宽松性等）导致的信息压缩与方向性偏移；（3）基于种族、性别、民族、外貌等非工作特征的歧视性偏好导致的绩效解释与评价的异质化转移。这些偏差可能单独或交互作用，使组织难以仅凭年终评分就准确区分员工表现，也容易将结构性不平等内化为“绩效结果”。<cite id="01211546-0">There exist severe problems in obtaining accurate supervisor ratings of job behavior, even on a single dimension; disagreement among raters signals error; bias and halo are fundamental, intractable sources of rater variance; people tend to rate those like themselves more favorably; halo forces raters to substitute a global impression across dimensions, and no instrument fully resists halo</cite><cite id="668e0e58-2">Halo, proximity, leniency and severity, contrast, central tendency, past-record anchoring, recency, rater attitudes, personal bias, and discrimination between inside/outsider and appearance are well-documented errors that contribute to idiosyncratic rater bias; generalizability theory decomposes rating variance into idiosyncratic and interrater-reliable components</cite>.

# 证据一：评价中的随机噪声与低一致性

多研究与元分析显示，尽管单个主管对某一维度的评分内部可信度可能较高，但不同主管对同一员工的判断差异显著，说明主要误差源自各自不同的感知与偏好（idiosyncratic rater effects）。例如，Viswesvaran 等的元分析（K=40, N=14,650）显示，同事间对“总体工作表现”评分的一致性仅为 0.52，而内部一致性与稳定性分别为 0.86 与 0.81；换言之，主管间差异是误差的主要来源。这类噪声在组织中造成“错觉式清晰”：评分看似精确，实则掩盖了大量不确定性，尤其在跨主管对比与晋升排序时易引发误判。<cite id="3792ad22-0">The most relevant finding was an interrater reliability of 0.52 for supervisory ratings of overall job performance (K=40, N=14,650), with stability 0.81 and internal consistency 0.86; this showed that the primary source of error in supervisory performance ratings arises from individual raters' idiosyncratic perceptions</cite><cite id="668e0e58-2">Generalizability theory partitions variance into idiosyncratic rater components (per rater, per ratee, per dimension, and unexplained) and interrater-reliable components, quantifying how much noise each source contributes</cite>.

# 证据二：系统性偏差如何压缩真实差异（光环、中心趋势、松紧偏差）

- 光环效应（Halo）：主管用单一突出印象推断其他维度，导致跨维度评分纠缠、信息失真。例如，一个“积极形象”可能抬高沟通、知识、努力等看似独立维度的评分，而真实表现未必均衡；反之，一次差错可能压低所有维度（devil’s horns）。这种替代使评价无法准确反映多维绩效，相当于人为模糊了表现图谱。<cite id="01211546-0">Halo error occurs when raters rely on a summary impression for each ratee rather than distinguishing levels across dimensions; many reports conclude no instrument is fully resistant to halo</cite><cite id="668e0e58-1">The halo effect lets one aspect influence other aspects; a negative halo or devil’s horns lowers ratings across dimensions due to a poor score on one dimension</cite>.

- 中心趋势偏差：主管倾向于将大多数员工评为“中等”，拒绝给出极端分数。这会抹平高绩效与普通绩效的分界，降低排名的有效性；在晋升排序中，本应拉开差距的评价反而趋于压缩，导致能见度不足与错配。<cite id="01211546-0">Central tendency leads raters to rate employees as average, reluctant to give very good or very bad ratings, causing variance loss within and between people</cite><cite id="668e0e58-1">Central tendency causes ratings to fail to discriminate within or between people</cite>.

- 松紧偏差（Leniency/Severity）：主管或整体偏松或偏严，系统性高估或低估表现。这种偏差可能与工作记录缺失、近期行为主导（recency）或个人价值观相关，进一步扭曲绩效排序。在缺乏文档支持时，主管依赖片段化记忆，易引入方向性误差。<cite id="668e0e58-1">Raters tend to be lenient (overstate performance) or strict (understate performance); recency error arises when appraisals rely on recent behavior without full documentation; central tendency rates many as average, reducing discrimination</cite><cite id="01245155-2">A substantial body of empirical literature demonstrates people tend to rate those like themselves more favorably</cite>.

# 证据三：身份与社会性偏差导致的绩效解释异质化（种族、性别、民族、外貌等）

- 相似性偏好与“光环”泛化：主管常因其与员工在价值观、风格或表面特征上相似而给出更高评价，这与光环机制相互作用，形成系统性优待。已有研究指出，人们倾向于按照自身偏好（如重视主动性、知识等）更积极地解读他人行为，且这种偏好可与光环叠加。<cite id="01211546-0">A substantial body of empirical literature demonstrates people tend to rate people like themselves more favorably; individuals rely on their own characteristics to judge others, affecting accuracy in identifying “correct” vs “incorrect” behaviors</cite>.

- 外貌与社会影响：实证研究表明，种族与性别交集（如女性与有色人种）的自我评价因社会影响与刻板印象而被压制，最终主管评分中女性与有色人种更可能被低估；当移除这种社会影响路径（不让自我评价传给主管）后，主管评分下降并部分弥合女性种群在第一年的评价差距。这直接证明了非工作特征通过社会性与认知偏差“转移”进评价中，并可通过流程干预部分纠正。<cite id="1cf7038d-2">Analyzing multi-national firm data, we find gender and intersectionality differences in self-ratings and race and intersectionality differences in manager ratings, leading to female employees of color being assigned the lowest final ratings; keeping self-evaluations from managers lowered manager ratings and closed the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year, though overall dynamics persisted; in the US, 22–28% of Black employees’ manager ratings would need increases to eliminate the race gap</cite>.

- 竞争性晋升证据：在真实企业数据中，当控制任职年限与绩效评分时，少数族裔女性仍比白人男性有更高的晋升概率（例如，技术序列中晋升到高级职位的“优势比”显著），说明在相同“绩效”标签下，结构性身份因素仍影响排序；同时，光环效应的普遍性也导致高绩效标签本身的解释存在异质性。这表明，若仅依赖年终评分作为晋升依据，可能将系统偏差“合法化”为“绩效结果”。<cite id="1cf7038d-0">White women had 79% higher odds of promotion to MGR2 than White men, net of performance rating and tenure; across technical levels, White and Asian women had advantage probabilities, while Black/Latinx/Native/Pacific Islander women had limited promotion despite presence in candidate pools with high prior ratings</cite><cite id="1cf7038d-1">Analyzing within-firm racialized promotion processes with longitudinal data reveals differences across levels; an “illusion of fairness” among higher-status groups coexists with systematic disparities, motivating interventions</cite>.

# 从评价到结果的“转移”：薪酬、晋升、培训的代价

当管理者依据噪声高、偏差多的评分做决策时，错误信号会被放大到人力资本配置中。元分析与实证研究共同指向：主管评分的跨人一致性不足（如总体绩效仅 0.52），却常用于排序与资源分配，导致随机噪声与系统偏差共同决定晋升与薪酬，使得真正绩效高的员工被低估、绩效适中的被误判为优秀、而受偏差优待者获得晋升。这种“转移”不仅造成效率损失（错配人力资本），更强化组织不平等的结构性与可见性问题。<cite id="3792ad22-0">Interrater reliability of 0.52 for supervisory overall performance ratings indicates substantial between-rater variance as the primary error source, implying that ranking and allocation decisions rely heavily on idiosyncratic noise</cite><cite id="01211546-0">Rater disagreement signals error; bias and halo remain intractable; people tend to rate those like themselves more favorably, embedding social bias into appraisal outcomes</cite><cite id="1cf7038d-0">Even after controlling for performance rating and tenure, White women have higher promotion odds, while Black/Latinx/Native/Pacific Islander women face barriers despite high prior ratings</cite>.

# 具体偏差路径与交互作用模型

绩效错觉转移的形成可归纳为两条作用链与交互效应：
1) 信息扭曲链：主管从观察到行为出发，受近期性、中心趋势、光环/恶魔角等认知捷径影响，将多维行为压缩为单维标签，并叠加个人偏好与相似性，最终输出失真的“绩效点数”；<cite id="668e0e58-1">Raters exhibit leniency/strictness, recency, and central tendency that reduce discrimination; halo and devil’s horns compress multi-dimensional performance into biased ratings</cite><cite id="01211546-0">Halo forces reliance on global impressions; no instrument is fully resistant to halo; raters vary in accuracy by personal characteristics</cite>.
2) 结构偏差链：组织文化与制度路径（如自我评价传递、绩效面谈框架、KPI设计）引导主管引入种族、性别、民族、外貌等非工作信号，这些信号通过相似性、光环泛化与刻板印象影响解释，最终进入排序与决策；当移除传递路径时，主管评分与种群差距相应缩小。<cite id="1cf7038d-2">Gender/intersectionality differences in self-ratings and race/intersectionality differences in manager ratings produce lower final ratings for women of color; removing self-evaluations lowers manager ratings and narrows the first-year gap for women of color</cite><cite id="01211546-0">Rater bias—preference or prejudice—undermines fairness; individuals selectively weight “correct/incorrect” behaviors by their own values, embedding systematic differences</cite>.
交互上，光环与中心趋势会放大相似性偏差：主管对“熟悉/一致”员工的积极光环更易滑向中等化，从而掩盖真实高绩效；对“不熟悉/不一致”员工则易陷入严格化或恶魔角，导致系统误判。这种耦合使得仅靠培训难以根治，需结构与流程并行。<cite id="01211546-0">Halo and central tendency jointly reduce discriminability and invite personal bias; training risks reducing accuracy and interrater reliability in opposite directions</cite><cite id="668e0e58-2">Training urging raters not to commit halo may reduce accurate differentiation and lower reliability; finer distinctions can also reduce interrater agreement</cite>.

# 组织应对：从设计、流程到治理的“去错觉化”策略

- 设计上“把不可见的变可见”：将多维行为转化为可核验的客观证据（KPI、项目成果包、客户评分、里程碑、代码评审、财务指标等），并用平衡计分卡或客户/同事/自我多源评分摊平单一主管视角的噪声；<cite id="3792ad22-0">High intra-rater reliability alongside low interrater reliability points to idiosyncratic perceptions as the main error source, suggesting the need to add multi-source evidence</cite>.
- 流程上“先证据、后评价”：强制要求主管在评分前提交可追溯的行为事例与数据附件；引入盲审机制或临时隐藏身份标签（如剥离自我评价的传递路径），以阻断非工作特征的渗透；<cite id="1cf7038d-2">Keeping self-evaluations from managers reduced manager ratings and closed the first-year evaluation gap for women of color, evidencing the role of social influence pathways</cite>.
- 技术上“量化偏差、动态校准”：建立评分校准模型，将主管评分与客观指标、历史一致性、跨主管对比进行比对，自动预警异常（如相同客观产出却显著高于同行、连续两年极端值、与自我评价方向冲突等）；<cite id="37979981-0">Rater-specific variance components (per rater, per ratee, per dimension, and error) from generalizability theory can guide targeted calibration and audit</cite>.
- 训练与反馈上“纠偏而非唯技术论”：认知偏差训练需与结构工具绑定；例如，教授识别光环与中心趋势的技术、使用行为锚定与对比校准表单，同时定期开展评分者间信度反馈与个案研讨，因为单纯训诫易导致“更细分类却更低一致性”的反效果；<cite id="01211546-0">Training urging raters not to commit halo may reduce accurate differentiation and reduce interrater reliability; making greater distinctions can also reduce interrater reliability</cite>.
- 治理上“透明化与问责”：对外公开晋升与薪酬决策的关键评分阈值与分布异常的校验规则；对连续出现异常偏差的主管启动个案审计，必要时引入独立仲裁与结构化申诉机制，防止“绩效幻觉”自我强化；<cite id="1cf7038d-1">Systematic disparities coexist with an “illusion of fairness” among higher-status groups, motivating governance that exposes and rectifies unfairness</cite>.

# 总结与实践意义

将绩效错觉转移拆解为噪声、系统偏差与社会性歧视三类机制，可以更清晰地诊断年终评分失真与晋升/薪酬错配的根源。证据显示，主管间一致性不足、光环与中心趋势压缩真实分布、相似性偏好与种族/性别/外貌等社会性偏差共同作用，已足以解释大量“看起来公平、结果却失衡”的组织现象。管理者若仅依赖年终评分的表面数字，可能将错觉转移为制度化的绩效正义；而引入多源证据、量化校准、路径隔离与偏差审计，方能逐步还原绩效信号、降低随机与系统误差的转移风险。<cite id="3792ad22-0">Interrater reliability of supervisory overall performance ratings is only ~0.52, implying substantial random and idiosyncratic error that can misguide allocation decisions</cite><cite id="668e0e58-2">Halo, leniency/severity, central tendency, and appearance-based bias systematically distort ratings; variance can be decomposed and targeted</cite><cite id="1cf7038d-0">Even with controlled performance and tenure, White women have higher promotion odds; Black/Latinx/Native/Pacific Islander women face barriers despite high prior ratings</cite><cite id="1cf7038d-2">Manager ratings reflect race/intersectionality differences; removing self-evaluation pathways narrows the gap in women of color’s first-year ratings</cite>.

# 局限与未来方向

现有证据多为横截面、组织级数据与特定行业案例；种族/性别对评分的因果边界、文化差异、远程协作与AI辅助评分的新场景下的偏差传导与治理，仍需更多纵向与跨文化实证。此外，如何在保留管理裁量与数据透明之间取得平衡、在提升一致性与避免“一刀切”之间设计弹性机制，是持续的实践课题。下一步可结合本行业数据开展评分者间信度审计、偏差热图与晋升回溯分析，以量化“错觉转移”的真实成本与改进步骤。<cite id="668e0e58-1">Raters’ leniency/strictness, recency, and central tendency reduce discriminability without documentation, underscoring the need for record-keeping and audit</cite><cite id="3792ad22-0">Low interrater reliability for overall job performance suggests that adding more evidence sources and calibration is essential to reduce error-driven transfers</cite>.

Title: Managers’ Perceptions of the Performance Appraisal System in the Local Municipality of Gauteng Province in South Africa
Snippet: In implementing performance appraisal, raters tend to make errors. There is a tendency for raters to be lenient or strict when giving ratings to ratees. In the former case, the rater overstates the performance of a ratee, that is, a ratee is rated higher than his/her actual performance. In the latter situation, the performance of a ratee is understated. A rate is given lower ratings than what he/she really deserves (Simmons, 2002). A recency error occurs when performance appraisal is based on the employee's recent behaviour, good or bad. The resulting performance review will be biased either favourably or unfavourably, depending on the way the performance information is selected, evaluated, and organised by the rater. Without work record or documentation for the entire appraisal period, the rater is forced to recall recent employee behaviour to establish the rating (Appelbaum, Roy & Gilliland, 2011). Cook and Crossman (2004) consider central tendency as a performance appraisal situation in which a rater tends to rate employees as average performers, thus becoming reluctant to give very good or very bad ratings. As such the ratings fail to discriminate either within or between people. 

Ratees' performance is considered to be the same irrespective of the different actual effort they exert. The halo effect is when a rater lets one particular aspect of an employee's performance influences the evaluation of other aspects of performance. Basically, a rater assigns ratings on the basis of a global impression of a ratee. In this case, a rater fails to distinguish among levels of performance on different performance dimensions. Conversely, a negative halo or devil's horns effect exists when the employee's ratings on all other dimensions is lowered inaccurately due to an accurate poor rating on one dimension (Grobler, Warnich, Carrel, Elbert & Hatfield, 2011).

Title: Manifestation of idiosyncratic rater effect in employee performance appraisal
Snippet: The other well-documented errors/effects, which are known to impact the variations in performance appraisals such as halo error, proximity error, leniency and severity errors, contrast error, central tendency, past-record anchoring, recency error, rater attitudes, personal bias and values discrimination between inside and outside employees, employee appearance, etc. (Javidmehr & Ebrahimpour, 2015), are also reasons that contribute towards the idiosyncratic bias of the raters on the performance appraisal of the candidates. Scullen, Mount, and Judge (2003) described the manifestations of rater effect by way of biases such as halo and leniency that have received widespread attention of the researchers in recent times compared to other cognitive biases. Halo error refers to the tendency of raters to allow an overall impression of a ratee to influence judgments along several quasi-independent dimensions (King, Hunter, & Schmidt, 1980), and leniency error is the rater's tendency to assign ratings that are generally either higher or lower than are acceptable by the ratees' actual performance. Hoffman, Lance, Bynum, and Gentry (2010) described idiosyncratic rater bias as a systematic effect that is common only to an individual rater but refrained from offering specifics. O'Neill, McLarnon, and Carswell (2015) identified the variance components in performance ratings based on generalizability theory (Cronbach et al., 1972), broadly classified the performance ratings' variances two discrete categories, i.e., idiosyncratic rater components and interrater-reliable components. The idiosyncratic rater components were further classified into four-folded rater-related variances identified by O'Neill, McLarnon, and Carswell (2015): 

1) variances due to rating differences concerning individual rater irrespective of the ratee or the dimension; 2) rating differences on a particular dimension, regardless of the ratee; 3) rating differences on a particular ratee, regardless of the dimension; and 4) unexplained variance. 

Despite having large literature on the idiosyncratic rater effect, the business world appears to be completely unaware of it.

Title: Meta-Analysis of Interrater Reliability of Supervisory Performance Ratings: Effects of Appraisal Purpose, Scale Type, and Range Restriction
Snippet: Finally, Rothstein's study (1990) is also relevant for the present reliability generalization study because she reported 37 individual coefficients of interrater reliability with their associated sample size and the variance of the ratings (which allows for the estimation of the µ-value for each study). When Rothstein's values are corrected for range restriction, the average interrater reliability is 0.64 for duty ratings and 0.69 for ability ratings. 

Concerning the meta-analyses of the reliability of job performance ratings, the most comprehensive one was carried out by Viswesvaran et al. (1996). They examined the interrater reliability of the performance ratings made by supervisors and peers, and also examined the internal consistency and stability of job performance ratings. They also estimated the reliability for overall job performance and nine facets of performance, including quantity, quality, leadership, communication competence, administrative competence, interpersonal competence, effort, job knowledge, and compliance with or acceptance of authority. The most relevant finding of Viswesvaran et al.'s meta-analysis was to show that the observed interrater reliability (sample size weighted) was 0.52 (K = 40, N = 14,650) for supervisory ratings of overall job performance. The stability for supervisory performance ratings was 0.81, and the internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) was 0.86. 

Taking into account that the different reliability coefficients assign different sources of variance to measurement error (Schmidt et al., 2003), Viswesvaran et al.'s (1996) results clearly showed that the intra-rater reliability coefficients of supervisory performance ratings were high (i.e., over 0.80) but that the interrater reliability was low (i.e., 52). Therefore, Viswesvaran et al.'s (1996) findings showed that the primary source of error in supervisory performance ratings arises from the individual rater's idiosyncratic perceptions of job performance. 

Two characteristics of Viswesvaran et al.'s (1996) metaanalysis must be mentioned. The first one is that their database included Rothstein's (1990) study, which represented about 75% of the total sample size of the meta-analysis.

Title: Meta-Analysis of Interrater Reliability of Supervisory Performance Ratings: Effects of Appraisal Purpose, Scale Type, and Range Restriction
Snippet: As the main purpose of this reliability generalization study was to determine the interrater reliability of the supervisory ratings of overall, task, contextual, and positive performance, only studies that reported an estimate of this reliability form were included in the analysis. Furthermore, in the final database, we included only studies reporting actual supervisory-job-performance ratings with real incumbents. In other words, we did not consider experimental studies, studies with simulated people, and studies with students. We also excluded studies reporting interrater reliability estimates of interview ratings, interrater reliability of assessment center exercises, and interrater reliability estimates of performance in simulated exercises. As we were interested in supervisory interrater reliability, the estimates had to be calculated using supervisory ratings and we did not consider interrater coefficients obtained from peers, subordinates, and observers. Also, we did not consider interrater coefficients obtained from a single supervisor supplemented by a peer or an observer. When studies reported a range of numbers of incumbents, we coded the smaller number to provide a more conservative estimate (e.g., Dunnette and Motowidlo, 1976;Campbell, 1986;Blickle et al., 2008). When an article or document reported data from two or more independent samples of participants they were entered into the meta-analysis as separate interrater reliability estimates (e.g., Dunnette and Motowidlo, 1976;Campbell, 1986). When a study reported interrater reliability estimates for the same sample obtained on different occasions, the most recent estimate served as data source for that sample (e.g., Gunderson and Ryman, 1971). When a study used two performance measures for the same sample at the same time (e.g., ranking order plus Likert scale; graphic ratings plus paired comparison ratings), the average of the interrater reliabilities was enter as the data source (e.g., Mandell and Adkins, 1946;Buel and Bachner, 1961;Thompson and Thompson, 1985). Handyside and Duncan (1954) reported an interrater coefficient that had been corrected for range restriction and we transformed it back to the observed interrater reliability. We also excluded 11 studies because the same coefficients had been reported in another paper included in the dataset.

Title: Meta-Analysis of Interrater Reliability of Supervisory Performance Ratings: Effects of Appraisal Purpose, Scale Type, and Range Restriction
Snippet: Range restriction was not a relevant factor in the estimates of the interrater reliability for this performance dimension. 

The last analyses we carried out were the comparisons among the average interrater reliability estimates for the four job performance dimensions in order to answer the question of whether some dimensions were more reliably rated than others. Consequently, we calculated the 95% confidence value of the difference between pairs of interrater reliability estimates. In other words, we compared the interrater reliability of overall job performance with the interrater reliability of task, contextual, and positive performance dimensions; we compared the interrater reliability of task performance with the interrater reliability of contextual and positive performance, and, finally, we compared the interrater reliability of contextual and positive performance. Table 5 reports the results of these comparisons. The 95% confidence values of the difference among interrater reliability estimates showed overall job performance was more reliably rated than the other three dimensions, followed by task performance. The 95% confidence values were positive in five cases out six. We did not find statistical differences between contextual and positive performance. Therefore, these findings supported the suggestion that some dimensions are more difficult to rate than others (Borman, 1979;Wohlers and London, 1989;Viswesvaran et al., 1996). From this point of view, our findings suggest that overall job performance is easier to evaluate than the other three dimensions and that the most reliable method is to evaluate overall job performance for research purpose ratings with a multi-item scale (corrected interrater reliability = 0.70). 

In summary, as a whole, the results of this interrater-reliability meta-analysis showed that the rating purpose is a moderator of the interrater reliability of overall job performance, task performance, and contextual performance, which confirmed Hypothesis 1. The difference size of the corrected interrater reliability for administrative ratings and research ratings was 0.24 in the three job performance dimensions, which in percentage is a difference of 53, 63, and 64% for overall, task, and contextual performance, respectively. The best estimates of observed interrater reliability were 0.56, 0.47, 0.43, and 0.48 for overall, task, contextual and positive performance dimensions.

documents.snippet:
Finally, Rothstein's study (1990) is also relevant for the present reliability generalization study because she reported 37 individual coefficients of interrater reliability with their associated sample size and the variance of the ratings (which allows for the estimation of the µ-value for each study). When Rothstein's values are corrected for range restriction, the average interrater reliability is 0.64 for duty ratings and 0.69 for ability ratings. 

Concerning the meta-analyses of the reliability of job performance ratings, the most comprehensive one was carried out by Viswesvaran et al. (1996). They examined the interrater reliability of the performance ratings made by supervisors and peers, and also examined the internal consistency and stability of job performance ratings. They also estimated the reliability for overall job performance and nine facets of performance, including quantity, quality, leadership, communication competence, administrative competence, interpersonal competence, effort, job knowledge, and compliance with or acceptance of authority. The most relevant finding of Viswesvaran et al.'s meta-analysis was to show that the observed interrater reliability (sample size weighted) was 0.52 (K = 40, N = 14,650) for supervisory ratings of overall job performance. The stability for supervisory performance ratings was 0.81, and the internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha) was 0.86. 

Taking into account that the different reliability coefficients assign different sources of variance to measurement error (Schmidt et al., 2003), Viswesvaran et al.'s (1996) results clearly showed that the intra-rater reliability coefficients of supervisory performance ratings were high (i.e., over 0.80) but that the interrater reliability was low (i.e., 52). Therefore, Viswesvaran et al.'s (1996) findings showed that the primary source of error in supervisory performance ratings arises from the individual rater's idiosyncratic perceptions of job performance. 

Two characteristics of Viswesvaran et al.'s (1996) metaanalysis must be mentioned. The first one is that their database included Rothstein's (1990) study, which represented about 75% of the total sample size of the meta-analysis.

documents.snippet: As the main purpose of this reliability generalization study was to determine the interrater reliability of the supervisory ratings of overall, task, contextual, and positive performance, only studies that reported an estimate of this reliability form were included in the analysis. Furthermore, in the final database, we included only studies reporting actual supervisory-job-performance ratings with real incumbents. In other words, we did not consider experimental studies, studies with simulated people, and studies with students. We also excluded studies reporting interrater reliability estimates of interview ratings, interrater reliability of assessment center exercises, and interrater reliability estimates of performance in simulated exercises. As we were interested in supervisory interrater reliability, the estimates had to be calculated using supervisory ratings and we did not consider interrater coefficients obtained from peers, subordinates, and observers. Also, we did not consider interrater coefficients obtained from a single supervisor supplemented by a peer or an observer. When studies reported a range of numbers of incumbents, we coded the smaller number to provide a more conservative estimate (e.g., Dunnette and Motowidlo, 1976;Campbell, 1986;Blickle et al., 2008). When an article or document reported data from two or more independent samples of participants they were entered into the meta-analysis as separate interrater reliability estimates (e.g., Dunnette and Motowidlo, 1976;Campbell, 1986). When a study reported interrater reliability estimates for the same sample obtained on different occasions, the most recent estimate served as data source for that sample (e.g., Gunderson and Ryman, 1971). When a study used two performance measures for the same sample at the same time (e.g., ranking order plus Likert scale; graphic ratings plus paired comparison ratings), the average of the interrater reliabilities was enter as the data source (e.g., Mandell and Adkins, 1946;Buel and Bachner, 1961;Thompson and Thompson, 1985). Handyside and Duncan (1954) reported an interrater coefficient that had been corrected for range restriction and we transformed it back to the observed interrater reliability. We also excluded 11 studies because the same coefficients had been reported in another paper included in the dataset.

Range restriction was not a relevant factor in the estimates of the interrater reliability for this performance dimension. 

The last analyses we carried out were the comparisons among the average interrater reliability estimates for the four job performance dimensions in order to answer the question of whether some dimensions were more reliably rated than others. Consequently, we calculated the 95% confidence value of the difference between pairs of interrater reliability estimates. In other words, we compared the interrater reliability of overall job performance with the interrater reliability of task, contextual, and positive performance dimensions; we compared the interrater reliability of task performance with the interrater reliability of contextual and positive performance, and, finally, we compared the interrater reliability of contextual and positive performance. Table 5 reports the results of these comparisons. The 95% confidence values of the difference among interrater reliability estimates showed overall job performance was more reliably rated than the other three dimensions, followed by task performance. The 95% confidence values were positive in five cases out six. We did not find statistical differences between contextual and positive performance. Therefore, these findings supported the suggestion that some dimensions are more difficult to rate than others (Borman, 1979;Wohlers and London, 1989;Viswesvaran et al., 1996). From this point of view, our findings suggest that overall job performance is easier to evaluate than the other three dimensions and that the most reliable method is to evaluate overall job performance for research purpose ratings with a multi-item scale (corrected interrater reliability = 0.70). 

In summary, as a whole, the results of this interrater-reliability meta-analysis showed that the rating purpose is a moderator of the interrater reliability of overall job performance, task performance, and contextual performance, which confirmed Hypothesis 1. The difference size of the corrected interrater reliability for administrative ratings and research ratings was 0.24 in the three job performance dimensions, which in percentage is a difference of 53, 63, and 64% for overall, task, and contextual performance, respectively. The best estimates of observed interrater reliability were 0.56, 0.47, 0.43, and 0.48 for overall, task, contextual and positive performance dimensions.

Title: Can gender and race dynamics in performance appraisals be disrupted? The case of social influence
Snippet: Managers’ subjective appraisals of their employees’ performance and employees’ selfevaluations might be affected by demographic characteristics. As self-evaluations are typically shared with managers before they rate employees, social influence may contribute to gender or race differences in performance ratings. Analyzing data from a multi-national firm, we find gender and intersectionality differences in self-ratings, and race and intersectionality differences in manager ratings, leading to female employees of color being assigned the lowest final ratings. We evaluate a quasi-exogenous shock leading to self-evaluations being kept from managers before they appraised employees. This intervention disrupted social influence to some degree, lowering manager ratings and closing the evaluation gap for women of color in their first year of employment. It did not change overall gender or race dynamics. Race dynamics were particularly pronounced in the US where 22-28% of Black employees’ manager ratings would have to be increased for this race gap to disappear. *Bohnet: Harvard Kennedy School, Cambridge, MA, USA. Strategies: (1) Make it require synthesis across organizational psychology + statistical bias literature - but that's still surveyable. (2) Require reconciling conflicting evidence about bias correction interventions - stronger, but need to ensure conflicts exist in literature. (3) Embed a false premise about causation - e.g., assume removing one bias type eliminates transfer effects, when in reality biases interact. (4) Require universal quantification - 'do ALL bias-correction interventions reduce transfer?' but this may be too easily answerable as 'no'. (5) Make it context-dependent - 'explain to a manager with no stats background' changes answer requirements. (6) Multi-step reasoning about interaction effects between bias types. The literature documents these biases separately but rarely synthesizes the specific causal pathways that explain residual gender bias after halo control, making this a reasoning challenge rather than a retrieval task.

Overview and definitions

In performance evaluation, the halo effect refers to rater tendencies to let an overall, often first-impression global judgment contaminate ratings of specific dimensions, producing spurious correlations across otherwise independent domains of behavior or ability.<cite id="da22cbb2-2">One of the most studied types of rater effects is the ‘halo effect’ in which an assessor fails to discriminate among independent aspects of behaviour; a first impression can influence all subsequent judgements, and strong performance in one domain (e.g., communication) can influence judgements of other domains</cite><cite id="da22cbb2-3">Halo occurs when an assessment of one aspect of a person’s achievement generalizes to another; even when achievement-relevant information is rich and separated by subject, ratings still show halo bias, supporting that teachers’ judgments can be manipulated to show this bias</cite>. Halo undermines validity by making ratings move together and compress variance, and it often operates when observational information is limited, pushing raters to generalize from sparse cues.<cite id="da22cbb2-2">Halo produces inappropriately similar ratings across items and threatens the validity of inferences from performance ratings</cite><cite id="da22cbb2-4">When limited to observe performance, evaluators rely on minimal information and a resulting impression strongly influences subsequent assessment; halo is common in performance evaluation and reflects an assessor’s inability to discriminate specific attributes</cite>.

Why gender gaps can remain even after “controlling” halo

1) Halo can be largely appearance- and impression-based, and gender cues (dress, color, grooming, androgyny vs. femininity) systematically shape perceived competence and warmth independent of task performance. Appearance-related cues can trigger halo-like spillovers that differ by gender and context, so interventions that only remove first-impression generalization may still leave gendered appearance-driven bias in the residual. For example, clothing and grooming influence perceived competence; professionally dressed targets are seen as more competent and dominant than casually dressed ones, with gender-by-context interactions where casual business attire helps men more than women and formal attire helps women more on dominance, indicating that non-performance cues systematically shift competence judgments along gendered pathways.<cite id="da22cbb2-0">Clothing and the halo effect are recognized in professional contexts; grooming and dress style can influence evaluator appraisals of competence; differential treatment based on dress style leads to different outcomes in employment and occupational success</cite><cite id="1a078103-1">A significant interaction between gender and clothing affects competence ratings; professional vs. casual clothing yields larger competence differences for men than women and vice versa for warmth</cite><cite id="1a078762-0">Formal attire increases perceived dominance (M=4.50 vs. 4.00 for casual), with actor gender and context interactions: in the business context, men in casual attire are rated as more dominant than women</cite><cite id="1a078103-2">Participant gender and target gender interact on competence ratings; male raters give higher competence ratings to opposite-sex targets, and clothing color (red) increases competence ratings for male targets</cite><cite id="1a078103-3">Clothing has a stronger influence on perceived competence for men than for women and a stronger influence on warmth for women than for men</cite>. Such gendered appearance-to-competence mappings can persist as “residual” bias once pure within-domain halo is mitigated by structured forms, because they are tied to social-cognitive stereotypes and cues present in work contexts (e.g., office dress codes, conference attire), not to the performance tasks themselves.<cite id="da22cbb2-0">Appearance cues trigger stereotypes about competence and success, with differential treatment by dress style producing occupational outcomes</cite><cite id="1a078103-1">Gender-by-clothing interactions on competence ratings persist even when stimuli are controlled</cite>.

2) Stereotypes map differentially onto warmth vs. competence, so residual gender gaps can reflect trait-based halo rather than performance-based differences. Classic gender stereotypes associate women with warmth/likability and men with competence/assertiveness; evaluations that integrate first-impression warmth or charisma into competence judgments can implicitly favor women’s warmth and men’s competence, sustaining gender gaps across roles and tasks.<cite id="da22cbb2-0">People draw inferences from facial appearance based on gender, age, and ethnicity; attractive people are perceived as ‘good’ via halo; stereotypes increase both positive and negative perceptions of social groups</cite><cite id="1a078103-2">Participant gender and target gender interact on competence ratings; patterns consistent with gendered stereotype-driven differences</cite>. When organizations “control” only for immediate performance behaviors, these stereotype-linked halo routes (warmth-to-competence or competence-to-warmth spillovers) remain, especially in subjective, ambiguous tasks where behavioral evidence is thin.<cite id="da22cbb2-4">Evaluators often lack full observation and over-rely on general impressions; halo is common and interferes with performance evaluation</cite>.

3) Gender gaps can emerge at construct- and rater-level heterogeneity, not just global halo, so “adjusted” ratings still reflect biased anchors or standards. Field and assessment-center evidence shows gender differences can appear at sub-constructs (e.g., leadership style, communication, interpersonal vs. technical) and by rater, implying that controlling global halo does not remove construct-level or interactional biases. In large-scale assessment centers, prior studies are mixed overall, but construct-driven analyses show gender differences can appear on specific dimensions and latent constructs, not just overall scores, suggesting that subjective evaluation standards and anchors can embed gendered expectations even when procedures appear standardized.<cite id="bec6c604-1">Empirical studies are split on overall assessment-center differences; construct-driven analyses reveal male–female differences on specific assessment-center constructs and latent means in a British Army officer entry setting</cite>. Moreover, rater-by-gender interactions are detectable: some raters systematically rate males and females differently, and differential item functioning by gender can be substantial, indicating that even standardized forms can encode rater-specific gender bias that persists after simple de-haloing.<cite id="bec6c604-2">A fixed chi-square test found significant rater-by-student gender bias (χ2(12)=50.4; p<.001); one rater gave markedly higher ratings to females than males (4.06 vs. 2.01 logits), demonstrating substantive measurement variation by gender</cite>. When behaviorally anchored scales still load on social image or effort/energy (e.g., “professional image,” “overall effectiveness”) alongside task behaviors, the anchors can reintroduce gendered cues of presentation and demeanor into competence judgments, leaving gaps in the residual.<cite id="bec6c604-4">Factor analysis of behaviorally anchored scales produced Core Technical Proficiency and an Effort/Professional Image factor; correlations in the .40s–.50s were concluded to reflect halo error; BOS shifts focus from judging behavior to counting frequency to reduce evaluative halo</cite>.

4) Objective-to-subjective rating shifts: controlling halo may reveal performance asymmetries that look like gender gaps. Sometimes, structured criteria and behaviorally anchored evidence make gaps clearer, not smaller. For instance, vignette-based severity ratings with dimensional anchors reduced the influence of gender or pathology stereotypes by anchoring to observable severity, improving fairness and discrimination accuracy; conversely, when global, non-behavioral anchors dominate, gender effects are more likely to remain. This means that apparent “residual” gender gaps after “controlling” halo may actually reflect better alignment with objective indicators, not the disappearance of bias.<cite id="bec6c604-3">When vignette measures provide dimensional severity structure and multiple vignettes, teachers’ errors shift from gender/pathology to severity; discrimination accuracy improved and errors were driven by severity, indicating reduced vulnerability to gender bias</cite>. Likewise, BARS/BOS aim to mitigate halo by tying ratings to observed behaviors and frequency, but they can be effort-intensive to construct and may still capture underlying effort/image constructs that are gendered in perception, so organizations must verify that anchors truly separate performance-relevant behaviors from non-performance cues.<cite id="bec6c604-4">BARS were developed to overcome graphic scale deficiencies but do not automatically yield better measurement; factor structures often retain effort/professional image factors; BOS requires indicating frequency of behaviors rather than evaluating them to reduce evaluative bias</cite>.

What “control” of halo typically does—and why gaps can remain

- De-haloing via training and structured forms reduces general impression contamination but cannot fully remove all non-performance cues and stereotypes embedded in evaluative anchors and standards. Rater training and behaviorally anchored scales help by separating ratings from first impressions and tying them to concrete behaviors; however, if anchors capture social image, communication polish, or “energy,” they can still invite gendered halo spillovers from dress, grooming, and presentation norms in the workplace.<cite id="da22cbb2-2">Halo is a cognitive bias where a general impression drives judgments across domains; interventions that reduce general impression influence aim to restore discrimination among specific behaviors</cite><cite id="bec6c604-4">BARS require effort and often still load on effort/professional image; correlations in the .40s–.50s were interpreted as evidence of halo error; BOS shifts away from evaluative judgments to frequency counts to improve properties</cite>.

- Measurement design changes the dominant bias source. Moving from global graphic scales to behaviorally anchored or severity-structured vignettes shifts variance sources from impression-based global appraisals to observable, dimensional indicators, which can shrink gendered stereotype effects and reveal true performance gaps. When gender effects vanish on severity-anchored items, their presence on overall ratings reflects residual impression and stereotype contamination in global graphics rather than performance differences per se.<cite id="bec6c604-3">Dimensional severity anchors reduced gender/pathology bias and improved discrimination accuracy, with errors driven by severity rather than gender</cite>.

- Halo control interacts with organizational context. Appearance norms, sectoral dress codes, and meeting etiquette (e.g., “professional attire”) provide gendered cues that evaluators map onto competence, so interventions must constrain or blind attire/grooming cues in evaluation contexts and emphasize objective, behavior-specific evidence across tasks and time windows.<cite id="da22cbb2-0">Clothing as a powerful nonverbal cue activates stereotypes and influences competence appraisals, with differential outcomes in employment success</cite><cite id="1a078103-1">Clothing and gender interact to alter competence ratings, implying that attire systematically shifts perceived performance</cite>.

Practical explanations for the persistence of gender gaps after controlling halo

- Appearance-to-competence mapping remains a route: even with instructions to rate specific behaviors, evaluators may unconsciously credit or penalize targets for competence based on attire, grooming, and styling, especially in client-facing or image-sensitive roles, sustaining gender gaps once performance tasks are equalized.<cite id="da22cbb2-0">Clothing and the halo effect shape competence perceptions and occupational outcomes</cite><cite id="1a078103-1">Gender-by-clothing interactions on competence ratings persist under controlled stimuli</cite><cite id="1a078103-3">Clothing influences perceived competence more for men and warmth more for women, indicating gendered cue sensitivity</cite>.

- Stereotype-integrated anchors and constructs: behaviorally anchored scales that include “professional image,” “presence,” or “communication effectiveness” can encode social-cognitive stereotypes, so raters generalize from impression-laden anchors to competence even when instructed otherwise.<cite id="bec6c604-4">Behaviorally anchored scales often load on effort/professional image and “overall effectiveness,” with correlations interpreted as evidence of halo error</cite>.

- Rater heterogeneity and interaction effects: different raters apply different standards and impression weights, producing gendered measurement bias that does not disappear after global halo is reduced; fairness requires monitoring rater-by-gender interactions and calibribrating anchors across raters.<cite id="bec6c604-2">Significant rater-by-student gender bias demonstrated that measurement variation by gender is substantive and not coincidental</cite><cite id="bec6c604-1">Gender differences can manifest at sub-construct levels and latent means, not only overall ratings</cite>.

- Construct-level differences by role and domain: in ambiguous or integrative leadership tasks, gender-linked preferences may shape ratings on interpersonal vs. technical dimensions, so “controlling” global halo exposes, rather than eliminates, role-specific gaps aligned with social expectations, not with raw performance per se.<cite id="bec6c604-1">Construct-driven analyses show male–female differences on assessment-center constructs in leadership, beyond overall scores</cite>.

How to make gender gaps shrink further after de-haloing

- Use behaviorally specific, frequency-based evidence and calibrate anchors to remove non-performance cues. Replace evaluative anchors (e.g., “professional image”) with neutral, observable behaviors and, where possible, count frequencies over time to reduce evaluative halo and stereotype spillovers.<cite id="bec6c604-4">BOS requires indicating how often each behavior occurs rather than evaluating the behavior, reducing evaluative bias; BARS require effort but do not automatically improve measurement</cite>.

- Blind or constrain appearance and charisma cues during rating windows. Because attire, color, and grooming systematically shift competence and dominance ratings along gendered lines, evaluate in attire-agnostic settings or blind attire/grooming cues and focus on task-specific behavioral evidence during the rating period.<cite id="1a078103-1">Clothing significantly alters competence ratings with gender interactions</cite><cite id="1a078103-2">Clothing color increases perceived competence for male targets</cite><cite id="1a078103-3">Clothing has differential effects on perceived competence and warmth by gender</cite>.

- Monitor and adjust for rater-by-gender interactions. Apply differential item functioning (DIF) and latent mean analyses to detect raters who systematically favor one gender; recalibrate anchors or retrain, and consider cross-rater calibration exercises to equalize standards.<cite id="bec6c604-2">Rater-by-gender bias can be quantified via DIF analysis and shown to be substantial; results may need cancellation to achieve fairness</cite>.

- Use severity-anchored, multi-vignette or multi-source evidence. Dimensional, severity-based measures reduce stereotype-driven error and improve discrimination accuracy, making it harder for gendered appearance or warmth cues to contaminate ratings and revealing true performance gaps or their absence.<cite id="bec6c604-3">Severity anchors and multiple vignettes shifted errors from gender/pathology to severity, improving accuracy and reducing bias</cite>.

- Communicate that “overall impression” includes only verifiable, task-aligned behaviors. Because first-impressions still contaminate ratings, make impression cues work for fairness: train raters to capture specific, recent, and observable behaviors, weight them by evidence strength, and schedule evaluations after periods that minimize attire- and charisma-driven impression formation.<cite id="da22cbb2-2">A general impression can drive all subsequent judgments; training aims to restore discrimination among specific behaviors</cite><cite id="da22cbb2-4">When observation is limited, evaluators generalize from minimal information; de-haloing seeks to counter this tendency</cite>.

What remains uncertain

Evidence is mixed on whether gender gaps exist overall and on which constructs they appear, especially in assessment centers and leadership-role simulations; construct-driven analyses detect differences at specific constructs, but effects can vary by domain, role, and rater set.<cite id="bec6c604-1">Prior studies are about evenly split on overall assessment-center differences; construct-driven analyses reveal gender differences on specific constructs and latent means</cite>. Likewise, while appearance-to-competence mapping is robust in perception studies, magnitude and direction can depend on context (formal vs. casual business settings), and stereotype content varies across cultures and industries, so de-haloing strategies need tailoring to local cues and norms.<cite id="1a078103-1">Contextual differences in clothing’s impact on competence and warmth by gender indicate domain sensitivity</cite><cite id="1a078103-2">Business context and clothing color systematically alter perceived competence and gendered patterns</cite>. Finally, behaviorally anchored systems can still capture effort or image; organizations should audit factor structures and anchor content for persistent halo-like factors before concluding bias is eliminated.<cite id="bec6c604-4">Behaviorally anchored scales often retain effort/professional image factors; correlations interpreted as evidence of halo error</cite>.

Bottom line

Controlling for halo reduces general-impression contamination, but gender gaps can persist because other non-performance cues (dress, grooming, color), stereotype-driven mappings (warmth-to-competence), and rater/construct heterogeneity continue to shape subjective judgments, especially in ambiguous tasks and image-sensitive contexts. Behaviorally specific, frequency-based evidence and attire-agnostic evaluation procedures are needed to fully decompress ratings and reveal performance with less residual gender bias.<cite id="da22cbb2-2">Halo generalizes first impressions to multiple domains and threatens inference validity</cite><cite id="1a078103-1">Clothing and gender interact to shape competence ratings, indicating persistent non-performance cue effects</cite><cite id="bec6c604-2">Rater-by-gender bias can be substantial and systematic</cite><cite id="bec6c604-4">Behaviorally anchored and observation-based scales reduce but do not automatically eliminate evaluative halo; design and calibration matter</cite>. In short, “controlling for halo” often reveals rather than removes gender gaps by shifting the rating system from impression-based global graphics to behavior-specific anchors; to make gaps shrink further, organizations must constrain the influence of gendered appearance cues and ensure anchors and raters encode performance, not social image.<cite id="bec6c604-3">Severity-anchored, multi-vignette designs reduce stereotype-driven errors and align ratings with observable severity rather than gendered bias</cite>.

Title: The sights and insights of examiners in objective structured clinical examinations
Snippet: One of the most studied types of rater effects is the 'halo effect' [7,13,[20][21][22]. The halo effect is a cognitive bias in which an assessor fails to discriminate among independent aspects of behaviour when making a judgement about a student [7,22]. For example, the halo effect may occur when an examiner makes a judgement based on a general impression, such as a first impression, which then influences all subsequent judgements or ratings. Another example of the halo effect occurs when a rater allows an individual's performance in one domain, such as communication, to influence judgements of his or her performance in other domains. Title: Halo effects in grading: an experimental approach
Snippet: Abstract Halo effects in teacher judgments, can occur when the assessment of one aspect of a person’s achievement is generalised to another aspect of achievement for that same person. We conducted an experimental study in which participants (N = 107) had to grade vignettes of the same student in two different subjects. The first vignette described either a weak, average, or strong performance, whereas the second vignette always described an average performance. Thereby, rich descriptions of achievement-relevant information were used, and the impact of influencing factors was reduced. The treatment condition emerged as a significant predictor of the grade given for the second vignette even after controlling for gender, status of the participants, and the gender of the student. The results suggest that participants’ ratings can be manipulated to show halo bias. The results support the view that teacher education should raise awareness of possible sources of the halo effect.

Title: A construct-driven investigation of gender differences in a leadership-role assessment center.
Snippet: The examination of gender differences in assessment centers has a long research tradition (Baron & Janman, 1996). The general conclusion from prior studies is a mixed one. Empirical studies are approximately evenly split between studies showing no significant differences between men and women and studies indicating that women scored somewhat higher than men. Unfortunately, the majority of past studies have examined gender differences only at the level of the overall assessment center rating (OAR), leaving open to doubt whether differences on particular dimensions, or constructs, led to final OAR differences. The findings of all previously published studies on gender differences in assessment centers are summarized in Table 1.

The aim of this study was to conduct a construct-driven examination of gender differences in assessment centers. This means that the present study focused on gender differences at the level of the assessment center constructs instead of at the more diffuse level of the OAR. We also aimed to advance prior research on gender differences in assessment centers in two other ways. First, from a substantive point of view, we generated a priori hypotheses about gender differences on these constructs on the basis of theoretical and empirical research on gender differences in leadership style (e.g., Eagly, 1987;Eagly & Johnson, 1990;Eagly & Karau, 2002). Second, from a methodological point of view, we used both effect size statistics and latent mean analyses to investigate gender differences in assessment center ratings. Specifically, male-female subgroup differences were examined in terms of both the observed (thus error-laden) dimension ratings by assessors and the latent constructs. The following section discusses each of these contributions in more detail. The setting of this study is a large-scale assessment center for officer entry in the British Army.
</snippet>

Snippet: His/her true performance might then not be visible (Schmitt & Chan, 1998, p. 79). 

To overcome the deficiencies of graphic rating scales (low reliability and poor discriminability), Behaviourally Anchored Rating Scales (BARS) were developed. Firstly, the major dimensions of job performance (five to ten performance dimensions) were determined. Thereafter, each of the dimensions was anchored by five to seven behavioural statements (Ployhart et al., 2006, pp. 180-181). 

In practice it was found that "although BARS require much effort and time to construct, they surprisingly do not result in scales with better measurement properties" (Ployhart et al., 2006, p. 181). Schmitt and Chan (1998, pp. 91-92) critically examined the structure of BARS. They developed ten behaviourally anchored scales and applied them to 467 investigative officers. The ratings were done by their immediate supervisors. The ten behaviourally anchored scales plus an overall dimension of effectiveness were intercorrelated and subjected to a factor analysis. Two factors accounted for 65% of the common variance. Recording and Writing, Making Presentations, Gathering Information, Analysing Information, Planning and Organising and Monitoring Work/Detail had substantial loadings on the first factor, which was identified as Core Technical Proficiency. The second factor had substantial loadings on Develops Relationships, Effort and Initiative, Professional Image and Overall Effectiveness. This factor was identified as Effort (Schmidt & Chan, 1998, p. 92). The authors found that "most of the correlations are in the .40s and .50s", and concluded that it is "evidence of halo error" (Schmidt & Chan, 1998, p. 91). 

In order to further improve the properties of graphic rating scales, Behavioural Observation Scales (BOS) were developed. They retained "the behavioral specificity of BARS", but raters were required to indicate "how often each behavior occurred". They were not required to evaluate the behaviour of the person (Ployhart et al., 2006, p. 182). 

Another variant of behavioural rating scales is the Mixed Standard Scales (MSS).

I will structure the answer with: definition/mechanism of halo; why gender gaps persist (appearance, stereotypes, construct-level effects, rater heterogeneity); what “control” actually does (structured criteria, BARS/BOS, training) and why gaps can remain; practical levers (objective behavioral evidence, de-biasing, calibration, blind/rating fairness checks); and uncertainties where domain-specific evidence is mixed.
